doc.title: Ray Shiner interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 11, 1998

chapter: Marriage and freelancing in New York
title: Studio dates and the unison flute story
summary: Sight-reading calls, each date an audition, and the A&R man correcting unison flutes with Romeo Penque and Phil Bodner.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Well tell me about working studio dates. You would get a call to come and they would specify what they wanted you to play, but you didn’t really know what the music was going to be.
Didn’t know anything until I got there.
And then you’d read it down.

Sight read it. That was the reputation you had to have before they’d call you to play a studio date. If you didn’t make it, the news would get around town that this guy bombs, and you wouldn’t get called again.

So each date was an audition. I was lucky. The musicians are very nice, and they’re very thoughtful and they’re very helpful. They would break their neck to help you. We had one date, I have to tell you this, the A&R man usually from the advertising agency, and a lot of times they imagine that they’re musicians. This guy thought he was a musician and he yelled in — we had five saxes there, we were all playing flute. We were playing unison flute, you know what unison flute is?

We’re all playing the same notes. This guy had to show that he knew something about music, so he hit the intercom button he says, “All right guys,” he says, “we’ve got to straighten something out.” He says, “The third flute there’s a couple of bad notes at Letter C.” We’re all playing unison, the same note. So I look at Phil, and he looks at me, and we both looked at Romeo, and these are the most famous doublers in New York City.

Now you don’t go any higher than that. And the three of us are looking at each other, and he said, “What kind of an idiot do we have in the control room?” Of course I don’t say this. Phil was the diplomat among the three of us. He says, “Let me handle it.” He says, “Give us a couple of minutes and we’ll straighten it out.” So he looks at me and he looks at Romeo and he says, [whispers] “Play the same notes.” So we played the same notes and the guy in the control room says, “That’s better.” So we took twenty minutes to do this, and we got twenty minutes overtime.
I can tell these stories now.
Well, I like to hear them.
Well this is a long time ago.
